The idea that we could somehow track these incredibly short-lived events that touched a vanishingly small group of people at all would have a meaningful trace that you could pickup at a granular level is a bit odd to me.

I think that's part of the excitement and wonder of this type of lost media. It perfectly captures a period/moment in time. We think we remember that time, but the details get smoothed over and lost in our memories. But many of those discrete details are captured on that old media. These old recordings are "of their time"... and for me it's fun to reach out and touch that past in a tangible way. To recognize how it still influences/echoes today.

For example, my father sort of casually played acoustic guitar his entire life. You know, taking the guitar out when sitting around the campfire and playing a few songs. Turns out he and his friends "made music" while in high school in the 50s. I'm pretty sure it was just them noodling in someone's basement. But about 10 years ago one of his old friends contacted him, they had found a reel-to-reel tape that one of them made while they were goofing around so long ago. And they digitized it and sent him the mp3. Was an incredible thing to be a fly on the wall listening to these 1950's teenagers jamming and talking/laughing with each other in the way they did back then.

I think preservation of lost media is critical for anyone trying to keep perspective in our modern age. Everything is so ephemeral now, and even nostalgia is repackaged and resold to us for profit or political influence. Lost media lets you experience some of it directly yourself, fly on the wall style, and I think it's one of the few ways we can keep a firm grasp on where we've come from, what we've lost, and what we've gained.

I mean to be completely accurate the Earth doesn't strictly orbit the Sun. Both the Sun and Earth orbit each other around a point at their "combined" center of mass, the barycenter - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barycenter_(astronomy). This is something you need to take into account for all the planets in the solar system and as a result, the "center" of the whole system is constantly moving. The solar system's barycenter is often not even inside the Sun.

I think that sort of proves the point that the OP was making, which is that you can create a functional model around any arbitrary location and it can be valid (as long as valid means: it can make useful predictions). When you put the center of the Sun at the center of the model, you still need your models to account for the "orbital wobble" happening as a result of the Sun doing a little dance with Jupiter (and all the other masses that orbit it) in the equations for the determining the relative positions of the Sun and Earth.

Using the Sun as the center versus the solar systems barycenter are both somewhat "arbitrary" in that way, and depend on what you're trying to do with the information - how accurate you need it to be, and how complicated you're willing to make the calculations to hit higher accuracies.

Realizing the exchange rate benefit, I got the idea of giving him $100 each month as an experiment; $500 Brazilian Reals.

I wanted to know if the extra money would help and if I could use the exchange rate to help my friend get to a better place in life. Sort of a UBI but not quite.

Now, $100 to me is a bit of money, but 500 BR to him was a crazy amount of money to be given.

Over six months, it allowed him to quit his job at McDonald's, get out of a financially unstable roommate situation, move closer to his family in his own place, and find a better job. He started dating again.

I told him I would commit to a year, but he actually said at the 6.5 month mark that he's doing so well that I don't have to keep giving him money.

Three years later he's still doing great. I have concluded from this that more money in our pocket always helps, but there is a certain responsibility (maybe in general) needed when a gift like that lands in our laps. It can be easy to blow it [2] but just as easy to use it to move life forward.

It has certainly made me more ..aware/appreciative of my privilege and (sometimes fragile) security.

I find the effort to find lost media interesting, personally. It might sound weird, but the ephemerality of these things is something I personally find a bit liberating.

I've performed in maybe 130-ish bands over the last 30 years almost none of which played more than 10-20 shows. I've put out a lot of recordings for other people, and am around a lot of folks who have put out a lot of recordings for a lot of people.

All that work was highly ephemeral and mostly lost as soon as the band stopped playing. If there were recordings at all, they probably ended up in a cardboard box in someone's flooded basement.

At times, it's been kind of odd to think about how far all that goes back in time, like, probably as far as there have been people playing music. The idea that we could somehow track these incredibly short-lived events that touched a vanishingly small group of people at all would have a meaningful trace that you could pickup at a granular level is a bit odd to me. It seems so impossible that when I don't have access to the specific musicians involved, the chance meaningfully following up on the history or finding artifacts like recordings or t-shirts seems improbable.

For instance, in the mid-60s in Texas there was a big swell of garage rock in the wake of the Beatles playing on Ed Sullivan. It seems like a measurable thing to me, insofar as I played a whole lot of music with folks who came out of that scene, specifically ex 13th Floor Elevator guys. Some of that work from those bands eventually went to get large enough to become visible, The Moving Sidewalks prefigures ZZ Top, for instance. And so it's a bit easier to track. And some of the folks in that scene had longer careers, I used to work for a guy named Jay Boy Adams, who still performs in Santa Fe.

All that happened before I was born in the late 1970s.

But as it was told to me there are many dozens of other groups that were trying similar kinds of music, to varying degrees of success, many of which are barely even remembered by the people who were in those groups. Which is relatable to my own experience- sometimes some old project will come back in a memory, 3-4 folks who were on the same page artistically for a moment but then moved on.

I personally enjoy that situation- it's been a long life and it's statistically only half-over, and the idea of forgetting even the bands I will perform with this month makes playing with them a lot easier. The stakes become so low that following whatever creative impulse becomes less of a feat of overcoming. At the same time, the music is both important enough that I can take hard-lines in my opinions and not have to worry about those boundaries biting me in the ass by preventing me from attaining some artistic recognition that will never come.

All that is kind of immaterial to what I was intending to respond, which is that unless you can find the folks who were in that band (which is not unlikely) your quest to find the other tracks will likely be fruitless. You would have a lot easier time finding Dave Laredo and company (whoever that is) personally.

The language is confusing for folks who haven’t experienced or researched the US immigration scheme. A few terms first:

* H1B visas are work permits issued to foreign-born workers sponsored by a company to work in the USA. These visas are bound to a specific employer with limited ability to transfer elsewhere, and on their own have ZERO ability to convert to a Green Card

* Green Card is Legal Permanent Residency (LPR), the first real step towards Naturalization. It lets you live and work anywhere in the USA, provided you generally contribute more than you receive in benefits (though this is very fungible depending on political incentives). Obtaining a Green Card is incredibly hard to do outside of family, with employer sponsorship being one of the few other viable routes.

So what seems to be happening here is that the regime wants to block Microsoft et al for applying for Green Cards for workers currently on H1B visas - not unheard of, but a rarity among the hordes of H1Bs employed yearly by technical firms. I suspect the goal is to discourage workers abroad from applying for H1Bs since employer green card sponsorship is off the table, but it won’t necessarily stop green cards via other routes (like marriage). title: Show HN: Abyss – ACP Agent Isolation with Middleware Support
text:
[Abyss](https://abyss.scurry.io/) is my take on a local-first agent containerization framework for ACP agents. It aims to neatly solve 2 issues:

1. Agents having full access to your desktop, and thus indiscriminate access to your files/secrets/etc.

2. Agent/harness features having to be re-implemented for each agent, even if the feature isn't tied to the specific agent in any way.

The former is largely self-explanatory, I think. I want to log into my bank, I don't want my agent to even have the ability. There's a fair bit of software in this space already. I'll loop back to the advantages of Abyss' containerization vs others in a second, but the 30,000 foot overview is that Abyss runs your agent in a Docker container and proxies the ACP connection so it works with Zed/Openclaw/whatever.

The second is the more interesting and novel (as far as I'm aware). The current zeitgeist is heavily agent-specific, even for features that only read/manipulate the context (which isn't agent-specific). If you want RAG, you're writing an agent-specific plugin. If you want subagents, you're writing an agent-specific plugin even though a subsession is really just context. As a user, that can leave you tied to a particular agent just so your plugins continue to work.

Abyss solves that by taking a page from Nginx's book. Abyss supports WASM-based plugins that have full access to read and manipulate ACP messages flowing back and forth. Plugins can hide secrets in prompts from users before the agent ever sees them, implicitly hydrate prompts with RAG, inject MCP servers and more. There's a diagram showing what the flow of messages look like [in the docs](https://abyss.scurry.io/docs/guides/04-plugins/02-developing...), and there's a sample plugin [in the repo](https://github.com/SethCurry/abyss/tree/main/plugins/secrets...) that will auto-cancel a session if the agent outputs an OpenRouter API key in tool calls and responses (sample screenshot [on this page](https://abyss.scurry.io/docs/guides/what-is-abyss/#i-am-not-...)).

Plugins currently only run on the host, mostly because I haven't written something to install/distribute them inside the containers that's better than an 8GB Docker image or forcing users to make a custom Docker image.

Current Features:

- Fully agent-agnostic: pre-build images exist for Pi, Hermes, Claude and Codex but it works with any agent that supports ACP

- Supports both bind-mounting host directories and having Abyss copy files in on startup (so the agent can see them but can't change your copy)

    - Includes pathing support to mount them at the same path as on the host so your `@file.md` references still work
- Supports startup scripts, so you can add Node/Go/Rust/etc to your agent container without having to write a Dockerfile

- Manages the full Docker lifecycle; point Zed at Abyss and Abyss handles creating/stopping containers, mounting directories, etc

- Agent containers can be ephemeral or persistent

    - Persistent containers leave the agent running; running Abyss will re-connect to a running container (or create one if it doesn't exist)

    - Ephemeral containers are created and then torn down every time you invoke Abyss, giving you a consistent environment for batch-type jobs
- WASM plugins allow creating functionality reusable across agents

Hi HN. I'm Joe, the solo developer behind this project. I left my consulting career 3.5 years ago; I became a farmer/rancher and have been diligently spending my remaining free time on this project.

The Nucleus stack is a few decoupled web technologies that work together as an implementation of the "ASO" architecture (stands for Adapter, State, Orchestrator). Practically, the goal of Nucleus is sophisticated, declarative, simple web apps with low-to-zero JS and no build process.

Architecturally, the "Orchestrator" is the primary innovation here. The original motivation: the web has never had an easy, native way to map data to the document. Every web framework primarily exists to fill this gap; most achieve it by keeping a copy of app state in JS memory and treating the DOM as a compile target. Yet CSS has quietly held templating-like abilities for a long time:

    span::before { content: attr(data-text); }
The "Orchestrator", dubbed "Quark", takes this idea seriously. It's a CSS derivative whose properties mutate the document, rather than style it. It can set attributes, iterate lists, stamp templates, listen for events, dispatch commands, run View Transitions, and more.

"Adapters" are certain elements (native or custom elements) that each bridge the "State" to one external protocol, such as fetch, form, history, WebAuthn, user gestures. They write only their own attributes.

"State" is simply the live DOM.

Two demos to take a look at; both have zero lines of app JS and no build process:

- The Todo demo on Nucleus' landing page is a fully RESTful app in about 30 lines of HTML, 20 lines of Quark.

- The Wrenfield PWA demo is a fictional, full-featured ecommerce site with polished features like SSG, SPA, hydration, web AR/3d models, WebAuthn, View Transitions, touch gestures. Try it on mobile to get a native-like experience. https://wrenfield.excom.dev

The Nucleus site itself is also dogfooding the stack. Opening up your inspector will show a highly declarative document, which is the live State of the app. Other examples are in the sidebar. The Nucleus stack is currently being used in production by a few companies. Open source versions of their apps are coming soon, as demos.

The stack differs from things you're probably aware of:

- HTMX - server owns logic and swaps fragments. Quark owns orchestration on the client, with the document as the only state.

- Lit and other web component frameworks - Custom elements are also part of this stack, and there can potentially be interop. But the ASO architecture advises elements to never render their own opinionated children or business logic. That is left to you.

- Datastar / Alpine - JS expressions or signals inside attrs. Quark lives in a separate, decoupled sheet and has no expressions with side effects. It does not call anything except your named pure functions.

- Blackboard pattern - architecturally, this is the closest relative. The site has an "Advanced -> Prior Art" page which discusses this.

The Nucleus stack is in beta. Here are the edges:

- Quark: unlike CSS, rules will not revert when they stop matching. You need to write the inverse, if needed. This is by design. Regardless, I'm currently exploring the architectural feasibility of rule reversion.

- Quark: certain pseudoclasses like :focus, :checked, :invalid are not observed.

- Quark and the elements rely on some fairly new browser APIs (like the Command API, Baseline 2025). Polyfills will be included in the first stable release.

- Will not play with React and certain other frameworks that lock the DOM to their own internal state. You will need a Shadow DOM as a boundary between them and the Nucleus stack.

Depending on the bundle/loading strategy you choose, the whole stack is somewhere between 1kb and a maximum of 70kb (brotli). This includes all out-of-the-box elements that provide generic functionalities like data fetching, lazy loading, and UI things like drawers, tabs, etc.

I am very keen on hearing feedback on this project. Particularly on the ASO architecture and the Quark language.

Nucleus will remain in beta for a few more weeks, as features are optimized and feedback is incorporated.

I don't know that any of this really matters. I could just as well say that you don't know anything at all about the internal experience of your dog's mind. All you can do is read behavioral patterns and attempt to make inferences. At best you have an approximation, and approximations tend to be wrong. Math is correct knowledge, not approximations of reality. Correctness is not a property of the idea or inference itself, since ideas and inferences can be wrong; it's the result of a verification process which you cannot possibly carry out in its entirety relating to the internal conscious experience of your dog.

We can dig into the philosophy of these definitions, but I think the far more interesting point is that even if we grant the existence of this kind of knowledge in the minds of human mathematicians, we have passed the threshold where that "knowledge" can keep up with systems that do not have access to it. Moreover, to claim humans have a "vast amount of mathematical knowledge" that is apparently valuable and that AI systems don't have, you'd have to prove that this "knowledge" is not implied or cannot be reverse engineered from the entire corpus of mathematical writing on which AI systems are trained. You'd also have to demonstrate that this "knowledge" leads to actual results that AI systems cannot generate without it. Given the results AI systems are producing, which are far beyond human ability at this point, it is more likely that AI systems have already internalized the entirety of this so-called "tacit knowledge" and then went much further, much faster, without humans in the loop at all.

Hi everyone, I'm a solo developer and I'm excited to share a tool I’ve been building and using for some time called VM Explorer. It’s a self-hosted control plane for managing Linux server fleets with application-level access control.

It all started with the most basic need- moving files in and out of my vms. I had Python HTTP servers running just to download/upload files(I'm not very fond of using scp). It was simple, but i still needed to log into SSH to check logs, start/stop services. I thought, why not have one single place for all of this?

That's how I ended up building a file manager with some basic file controls over HTTPS, accessible through any web browser. But I couldn't leave it open to the public, so I started building proper authentication, roles, and permissions system around it. and before i knew it, VM Explorer took shape.

I've been using it for a couple of months for my own personal use and at work, and it made things incredibly convenient for me. So, i thought it was time to share it with the world. I would love to hear your thoughts. The website has a live demo mode which lets you try it out without logging in, so please give it a spin!

A quick overview of core features VM Explorer have:

- Services, Disks & Processes monitoring & management.

- Web-based PTY terminal, built on nodePty. (upto 4 split terminals as once, each can run as different users from different servers).

- A full file manager (w/ files viewer/editor), allows cross-VM transfers. You can add as many servers as you want and transfer data between them directly (no FTP/SFTP, just direct download/upload over HTTPS, authenticated using your jwt tokens). You can also generate temporary, expiring public download links for any file/folder.

- Granular access control, create application-level users in seconds and restrict them to specific directories or specific system users (for the terminal). No need to manage SSH keys or user accounts on every server.

- Audit Logs, saved locally in SQLite, but you can export them or pipe them manually, on schedule or in real-time to Postgres, MySQL, MongoDB, or Webhooks.

Tech Stack:

- The daemon runs as a root systemd service. All communication between the backend and frontend is done over secure HTTPS (multi-SAN self-signed certs are auto-generated, and you can update your own cert paths anytime in /etc/vm-explorer/.env).

- Backend is built with Fastify (node.js/typeScript) and uses local SQLite to store the app's data.

- Frontend is built with React.js, SCSS, and Tailwind. It's also configured as a PWA if you want to install it as a standalone app on your desktop or mobile.

I've gone with a lifetime licensing approach because let's be honest neither of us would want to pay a monthly subscription for this kind of utility tool. So yeah, one time payment and you get to use it for life. I do plan on keep adding features to it and will support the existing users with bug/feature updates for atleast my lifetime.

Pricing:

- $49.99 - Solo (1 VM)

- $99.99 - Pro (5 VMs)

- $249.99 - Cluster (20 VMs)

For security conscious people, I want to clarify that the app works solely on your own system, it only ever interacts with my server in only these cases:

- License Activation/Deactivation

- A one-time license key validation once the license key is 30-days old (after which it is permanent, even if you later choose to deactivate and activate it in another machine).

- App Updates (totally optional)

- Any bug reports if you choose to send them (also optional, only what you write in the message is sent, I don't collect any system logs or any data).

All of these (except one-time validatation) are initiated by users directly.
